blocks.text: The Hebrews call the mouse עכבר achbar, a word that is perhaps rather Chaldee, and which properly means field mouse. For עכבר achbar seems to be said for עכלבר achalbar, with the L elided, as in the words Babel for Balbel, and Samuel for שאול-מאל Saul-meel, as if you were to say asked of God. For in Chaldee עכל achal is to consume; and בר bar is field: therefore עכלבר achalbar, and by contraction עכבר achbar, is consumer or devastator of the field ^{(1)}. The name fits the field mouse very well, which is a sure plague of the fields. Aristotle, Hist. book 6, ch. 37: Ἀπορεῖται δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν ἐπιπολαζόντων μυῶν γένεσις ἐν ταῖς χώραις, καὶ ἡ φορά. πολλαχοῦ γὰρ εἴωθε γίνεσθαι πλῆθος ἀμύθητον τῶν ἀρουραίων, ὥστε ὀλίγον λείπεθαι τοῦ σίτου παντός. γίνεται δὲ οὕτω ταχεῖα ἡ φορὰ, ὥστε ἔνιοι τῶν μὴ μεγάλας γεωργίας ἐργαζομένων, τῇ προτέρᾳ ἰδόντες ὅτι θερίζειν ὥρα, τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ἕωθεν ἄγοντες τοὺς θεριστὰς, καταβεβρωμένα ἅπαντα καταλαμβάνουσιν. [Aporeitai de kai hē tōn epipolazontōn myōn genesis en tais chōrais, kai hē phora. pollachou gar eiōthe ginesthai plēthos amythēton tōn arouraiōn, hōste oligon leipethai tou sitou pantos. ginetai de houtō tacheia hē phora, hōste enioi tōn mē megalas geōrgias ergazomenōn, tē protera idontes hoti therizein hōra, tē hysteraia heōthen agontes tous theristas, katabebrōmena hapanta katalambanousin.] The generation and increase of the mice that appear in the fields is also called into question. [II, 430] For often so great a multitude of field mice arises that little grain is left. And their increase is so sudden that some of those who have not ploughed much land, having decided the day before to reap, on bringing the reapers early the next morning find all the crops consumed. Hence Pliny, having spoken of the prodigious fertility of mice, book 10, ch. 65, says: And so it ceases to be a wonder whence so great a multitude of field mice ravages the harvests. And in Horus, book 1, ch. 47: the Egyptians, ἀφανισμὸν δηλοῦντες, μῦν ζωγραφοῦσιν, ἐπειδὴ πάντα ἐσθίων μιαίνει καὶ ἀχρηστοῖ [aphanismon dēlountes, myn zōgraphousin, epeidē panta esthiōn miainei kai achrēstoi], signifying destruction, paint a mouse, because in consuming everything it defiles and ruins it.

Examples are met with everywhere. Thus at 1 Sam. V, 6. in the Greek version it is written of those Philistines who held the captured ark: Μέσον τῆς χώρας αὐτῆς ἀνεφύησαν μύες [Meson tēs chōras autēs anephyēsan myes]. And in the Vulgate: And the villages and fields in the midst of that region boiled up, and mice were born. And again at ch. VI, 1. in the Greek: Καὶ ἐξέζεσεν ἡ γῆ αὐτῶν [col. 1018] μύας [Kai exezesen hē gē autōn myas]. And their land boiled up with mice. These are indeed glosses, since neither the Hebrew original nor the other versions, the Chaldee, I mean, the Syriac and the Arabic, recognize anything of the kind. Yet the thing is true in itself. For in verse five of the same sixth chapter the Hebrew too has: You shall make, etc. צלמי עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ, images of your mice that ravage the land; مثال الجرذان التي تسلطت علي الارض لتفسدها [mithāl al-jirdhān allatī tasallaṭat ʿalī al-arḍ li-tufsidahā], images of the mice ^{(2)} that fall upon the land to ravage it, as the Arabic translator has it. Accordingly Josephus, Antiquities book 6, chapter 1, rightly says: Τὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς χώρας μυῶν πλῆθος, ἀνελθὸν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς, κατέβλαψε, μήτε φυτῶν, μήτε καρπῶν ἀποσχόμενον· [Ta de epi tēs chōras myōn plēthos, anelthon apo tēs gēs, keteblapse, mēte phytōn, mēte karpōn aposchomenon] And a multitude of mice, emerging from the earth, laid waste what was in the region, sparing neither plants nor fruits. And Philastrius, on the Musorites: When the ark of the Covenant had been captured by the Allophyli, and the earth, through the wrath of God, had produced shrews, so that their crops perished. And Maginus in his Palestine: In some places of Palestine the fields are almost deserted because of the abundance of mice and shrews, so that, if certain birds did not devour them, the inhabitants could make no sowing ^{(3)}.

[II, 431] Lest anyone think this evil peculiar to Eretz Yisrael, Strabo, book 3, records that in Spain too there has sometimes arisen μυῶν πλῆθος, ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ λοιμικαὶ νόσοι πολλάκις ἠκολούθησαν [myōn plēthos, aph᾽ hou kai loimikai nosoi pollakis ēkolouthēsan], a multitude of mice, which has often been followed by a pestilential plague. And in Cantabria the Romans, a reward being offered, μυοθηροῦντες πρὸς μέτρον ἀποδειχθὲν διεσώζοντο μόλις [myothērountes pros metron apodeichthen diesōzonto molis], hunting mice to a fixed measure, were scarcely saved. Nor are there lacking those who report the same of Italy. Diodorus, book 3: Περὶ τὴν Ἰταλίαν μυῶν πλῆθος ἀρουραίων. ἐγγενηθὲν τοῖς πεδίοις, ἐξέβαλέ τινας τῆς πατρίου χώρας· [Peri tēn Italian myōn plēthos arouraiōn. engenēthen tois pediois, exebale tinas tēs patriou chōras] Around Italy a multitude of field mice, having emerged from the fields, drove some people from their native soil. This very thing is in Aelian, History book 17, ch. 41. And both follow Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 28. Further, it is most likely that the people of Cosa are meant, because Rutilius Rufus sings of Cosa:
The citizens, it is said, once forced to emigrate, abandoned their homes, infested by mice.
